children: U.S. stocks rose as oil futures tumbled on hopes of a resumption in U.S.-Iran negotiations, causing a relief rally that pushed high-risk technology stocks to record highs.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 366.19 points, or 0.71%, to 52048.83. The S&P 500 gained 114.20 points, or 1.49%, to 7764.70 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite added 599.55 points, or 2.26%, to 27122.09, a record high. It was the Nasdaq's first record close since June 2, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

Oil futures fell $4.52, or 4.5%, to $95.78 a barrel. President Donald Trump signalled an openness to meeting Iranian officials coming to New York for a gathering of the United Nations General Assembly. That offset the market impact of continuing attacks on Saudi Arabian infrastructure from Houthi fighters in Yemen.

Weighing on oil futures was "the fact the U.S. refrained from joining in with the Saudis and proposed a meeting with the Iranian leadership," said J.D. Joyce, president of Houston financial advisory Joyce Wealth Management. "It's still a very fluid situation...I'd be surprised for it to be over any time soon, but any positive indication is well received by the market."

The retail price of diesel touched record highs at an average $6.51 a gallon in the U.S., according to the American Automobile Association, or AAA. Congressional leaders proposed a ban on U.S. exports of the fuel, widely used by farmers, truckers and shipping lines.
Concerns about inflation and the policy response kept Treasury yields near multiyear peaks.

The yield on the two-year Treasury rose 0.009 percentage point to 4.751%, the highest close since July 1, 2024. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note declined 0.033 percentage point to 4.962%. The yield on the 30-year bond fell 0.031 percentage point to 5.296%.
The U.S. dollar ticked up against rivals after Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said the central bank could no longer afford to wait out energy shocks.
Rate-sensitive gold futures lost $40.10, or 0.9%, to $4345.80 a troy ounce.
Traders returned to bets on a prolonged AI boom as fears about "extinction risk" faded. Chip makers, viewed as big winners from the wave of data-center development, were particularly strong.
Advanced Micro Devices rose 9.9% to $615.52, topping $1 trillion in market capitalization for the first time.

Anthropic plans to stage its multibillion dollar initial public offering in November, later than many investors expected, reflecting the recent call for a slowdown in the development of AI technology from leading firms.
Nvidia struck a deal with Swedish autonomous-truck maker Einride to support an increase of self-driving vehicle production.

Shares of Warner Bros Discovery rose 11% to $30.80 for its biggest gain in almost a year after reports that Paramount reached an antitrust settlement deal with 12 state attorneys general, clearing the way for an $81 billion acquisition that will unite two of Hollywood's defining studios. Under the terms of the settlement, Paramount is likely to retain control of cable channels while committing to investment in domestic studios and production.

Major television networks agreed on Monday to suspend a rotation of broadcast journalists who cover President Trump after the White House removed CNN from a planned assignment covering the president's trip to New York.

The Trump administration proposed investing $5 billion in a new fund that would help Middle East countries rebuild energy infrastructure damaged as a result of the Iran war, and as a way to reduce their reliance on the Strait of Hormuz to transport oil and gas.
